'''Willem van Zeist''' (12 March 1924 – 7 October 2016) was a Dutch [[Archaeobotany|archaeobotanist]] and [[Palynology|palynologist]]. He was the director of the ''Biologisch-Archaeologisch Instituut'' at the [[University of Groningen]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://viagabina.rice.edu/paleobotanical/paleobotanical.html |last=Widrig |first=Walter M. |title=The Via Gabina Villas Sites 10, 11 and 13 |publisher=Walter Widrig and Rice University |year=2002 |accessdate=14 March 2011}}</ref>

==Education==
[[Van (Dutch)|Van]] Zeist studied biology at the [[University of Utrecht]], completing his PhD dissertation in 1955 on pollen analysis investigation in the Netherlands, with special reference to archaeology (''Acta Botanica Neerlandica 4'', 1955).<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wfhEAAAAMAAJ&q=Willem+van+Zeist+palynology |last=Van Zeist |first=Willem |title=Pollen analytical investigations in the northern Netherlands: with special reference to archaeology |publisher=North-Holland Pub. Co. |year=1955}}</ref> From 1951 to 1989 he was linked to the ''Biologisch-Archaeologisch Instituut'' at the [[University of Groningen]]. He became lecturer there in 1967 and a professor in 1973.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |url=https://www.geheugenvandrenthe.nl/zeist-willem-van |title=Willem van Zeist |website=Encyclopedie Drenthe |access-date=2017-01-12}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://hoogleraren.ub.rug.nl/hoogleraren/2042-zeist-willem-van  |title=Willem van Zeist (1924) |publisher=University of Groningen  |date= }}</ref>

== Research ==

===Europe===
Van Zeist conducted research in Europe on the oldest recovered [[canoe]] in the world, the [[Pesse canoe]]<ref>{{Citation |last1 = Van Zeist |first1 = W. |title = De steentijd van Nederland |journal = Nieuwe Drentse Volksalmanak |volume = 75 |pages = 4–11 |year = 1957}}</ref> found in the Netherlands.<ref name="CMC">{{cite web |url=http://www.civilization.ca/media/docs/pr148beng.html |title=The Mysterious Bog People - Background to the exhibition |publisher=Canadian Museum of Civilization Corporation |date=2001-07-05 |accessdate=2009-06-01}}</ref> According to [[Radiocarbon dating|C14 dating]] analysis it was found to be constructed somewhere between 8200 and 7600 BC.<ref name="CMC"/> This canoe is exhibited in the [[Drents Museum]] in [[Assen]], Netherlands.<ref name=":0" />

Van Zeist studied the vegetational history and peat bogs of southeastern [[Drenthe]] and concluded that Neolithic settlements had begun there around 5000 BC. He also concluded that the [[prehistoric]] disc [[wheel]]s found in the Netherlands dated to at least the Neolithic period.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://dissertations.ub.rug.nl/faculties/arts/1964/j.d.van.der.waals/ |last=van der Waals |first=Johannes Diderik |title=Prehistoric disc wheels in the Netherlands |publisher=Rijksuniversiteit Groningen (University of Groningen)|year=1964 |accessdate=14 March 2011}}</ref> Van Zeist also conducted analytical studies of [[pollen core]]s and charred seeds and fruits from archaeological excavations at [[Gasselte]], [[Noordbarge]], [[Odoorn]], Peelo and [[Wijster]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.encyclopediedrenthe.nl/Zeist,%20Willem%20van |title=Zeist, Willem van |publisher=Encyclopedie Drenthe Online |language=Dutch |accessdate=14 March 2011}}</ref> In 1983 he became a member of the [[Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.knaw.nl/en/members/members/5054 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150720182411/https://www.knaw.nl/en/members/members/5054 |title=Willem van Zeist |publisher=Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences |date= |archive-date=20 July 2015}}</ref>

===Near East===
[[File:Usdaemmer2.jpg|thumb|Van Zeist analysed the earliest known cultivated [[Emmer|emmer wheat]], from [[Tell Aswad]]]]
In 1975, van Zeist began work on establishing the climatological record for the Near East with pollen analyses from [[Iran]] and [[Turkey]]. Along with other studies he concluded that there had only been relatively minor fluctuations in the climate of this area since 5500 [[Before Christ|BC]].<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ESgZAQAAIAAJ&q=The+Oxford+Encyclopedia+of+Archaeology+in+the+Near+East |last=Meyers |first=Eric M. |title=The Oxford Encyclopedia of Archaeology in the Near East |pages=37&ndash;38 |isbn=0-19-506512-3 |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=1997}}</ref> He conducted paleobotanical studies and dating analyses at various Near Eastern archaeological sites such as [[Tell Ramad]], [[Tell Ghoraife]], [[El Kowm (archaeological site)|El Kowm]], [[Ras Shamra]], [[Cayonu]], [[Ganj Dareh]], [[Mureybet]] and [[Tell Aswad]]. At the latter site near Mount Hermon in [[Syria]], he made a find of the earliest cultivated [[Emmer]] Wheat yet found anywhere on [[Earth]] to date, along with what he considered to be domesticated [[pea]]s and [[lentil]]s along with other grains such as [[einkorn]] and [[barley]] at later stages.<ref>Miller, Naomi F. ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=Sl8w4FwWi48C&dq=Van+Zeist+and+Bakker-Heeres+aswad&pg=PT57 The Origins of Plant Cultivation in the Near East]'', in ''The Origins of Agriculture: An international perspective'', edited by C. Wesley Cowan, Patty Jo Watson, Nancy L. Benco. University of Alabama Press, 2006. P. 48.</ref>
